nodes.label: Last Artaxiads and Roman nominees
nodes.full: After Tigranes IV and the queen Erato the Armenian throne passed through a series of nominees of Rome and Parthia: Artavasdes IV, Tigranes V, Vonones, and in AD 18 Zeno, crowned by Germanicus as Artaxias III. The nobility, torn between the two powers, would not accept a king strong enough to rule, and the Artaxiad house died out.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 2.3–4, 2.56, 6.31–37; Josephus, Antiquities 18.52; Robert Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

nodes.label: Tiridates I
nodes.full: Tiridates, a brother of the Parthian king Vologases I, was put on the Armenian throne in 54 or 58, was driven out by Corbulo in 58–60, and in a compromise confirmed at Rhandeia in 63 was accepted by Rome as king, receiving his crown from Nero in Rome in 66. The Arsacid line he founded ruled Armenia with breaks for almost four centuries.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 13.34–41, 15.1–31; Cassius Dio 63.1–7; Suetonius, Nero 13; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Arsacid kings
nodes.full: In the second century a line of Arsacid kings, Sanatruk, Axidares, Sohaemus, Vologases and Khosrov I, ruled Armenia as Roman clients with periods of Parthian dominance, and Trajan's annexation of 114 and Verus's war of 163 interrupted it. Their order is uncertain, and rests on coin evidence and sparse literary mentions.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 68.17–20, 71.3; Hewsen 2001; Nina Garsoïan in R. Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 1 (1997).

nodes.label: Tiridates III
nodes.full: Tiridates III (Trdat), whom Diocletian helped to the throne in about 287 after the Persian conquest of Armenia and the murder of his father Khosrov II, was confirmed by Nisibis in 298 and, according to tradition, became a Christian under Gregory the Illuminator and made the faith the religion of his kingdom. His date for the conversion, 301 in Armenian tradition, is probably some years later.
nodes.src: Agathangelos, History of the Armenians; Faustus of Byzantium, Epic Histories; Garsoïan 1997; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Khosrov III to Arshak II
nodes.full: A fifty-year line of Arsacid kings from Khosrov III through Tiran and Arshak II struggled to keep Armenia independent of Persia: Tiran was blinded by Shapur II, Arshak II, who ruled for nearly two decades, was drawn into the Roman–Persian war and was seized by Shapur II and held in the Persian fortress of Anyush (the Fort of Oblivion), where he is said to have died, about 368.
nodes.src: Faustus, Epic Histories 4.14–55; Ammianus Marcellinus 27.12, 30.1–2; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Pap and partition
nodes.full: Arshak's son Pap was raised to the throne in 370 by Valens's troops and was murdered at Roman instigation in 374; the kings that followed, Varazdat, Arshak III and Khosrov IV, ruled under Mamikonian control until Rome and Persia divided the country in 387. Arshak III in the Roman fifth and Khosrov IV in the Persian four-fifths were the first rulers of the divided kingdom.
nodes.src: Ammianus 30.1; Faustus 5.32–38; Garsoïan 1997; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: End of the monarchy
nodes.full: In the Persian part Khosrov IV, Vramshapuh (c. 389–414) and then the ephemeral Artashes IV (Artaxias IV) ruled until in 428 the nobles, tired of the king, asked the Persian king to depose him; Bahram V did so and put a Persian governor, a marzban, in his place. In the Roman part the last king died in 389 and no successor was appointed.
nodes.src: Moses Khorenatsi, History 3.64; Faustus 6; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Pharasmanes and Iberia
nodes.full: In the first century Iberia was ruled by Pharasmanes I, who as a client of Rome placed his brother Mithridates and then his son Rhadamistus on the Armenian throne and fought Parthian-backed rivals. In the second century Pharasmanes II visited Antoninus Pius, who gave him an equestrian statue and enlarged his realm. Roman inscriptions at Mtskheta show Rome's influence.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 6.32–35, 12.44–51; Cassius Dio 69.15, 70.2; Vespasian inscription at Mtskheta (Harmozica), AD 75; Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).

nodes.label: Mirian III
nodes.full: The Georgian chronicles call the founder of the Chosroid dynasty, which replaced the Arsacid line of Iberia in the third century, Mirian III; he was king in the years of the Persian wars and of the conversion of Iberia to Christianity. His successors reigned as vassals of Persia or Rome in turn, including Sauromaces and Aspacures, appointed by the two powers in the 360s.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 1.10; Ammianus 27.12; Toumanoff 1963; Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

nodes.label: Kings of Albania
nodes.full: Caucasian Albania, between the lower Kura and the Caspian, was ruled by its own kings, a line apparently of Arsacid origin by the fourth century, who first appear by name in Armenian and Persian sources and ruled over a mixed population of Albanian tribes. The kingdom fell under Sasanian control in the third century, as Shapur I's inscription shows, and its dynasty is recorded in an Armenian history.
nodes.src: Shapur I, Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ); Movses Kaghankatvatsi, History of the Albanians; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Corbulo
nodes.full: Nero's general Corbulo, with Syrian and Cappadocian legions, captured and burned Artaxata in 58 and Tigranocerta in 59, installed Tigranes VI, and in 62–63 after the defeat of Paetus at Rhandeia reached a settlement with Vologases, under which Tiridates became king of Armenia on condition that he receive the diadem from the Roman emperor.

nodes.label: Rhadamistus
nodes.full: The Iberian prince Rhadamistus, with his father's army, invaded Armenia in 51, killed its king Mithridates, his uncle, and was in turn expelled by the Parthians in 52; the episode shows the Iberian kings as arbiters of Armenian affairs, and Tacitus tells it at length.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 12.44–51.

nodes.label: Trajan’s province
nodes.full: In 114 Trajan occupied Armenia after the Parthian king's nominee Parthamasiris refused to accept the crown from Rome; he organised it as a province, and in the same year received the submission of Iberia and Albania in the east. His successor Hadrian withdrew from the province and restored a client king.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 68.17–20; Eutropius 8.3; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Verus and Artaxata
nodes.full: When Vologases IV placed his own king on the Armenian throne in 161, the legions of Statius Priscus invaded, took and razed Artaxata in 163 and built a new capital, Kainepolis ('New City', Vagharshapat), where Sohaemus was installed as king. The war was part of the Parthian war of Lucius Verus.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 71.3; Historia Augusta, Verus 7; Lucian, How to Write History 20.

nodes.label: Shapur I
nodes.full: The Sasanian king Shapur I, in the inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht at Naqsh-e Rostam, names Armenia, Iberia and Albania among the lands he subdued; in Armenian tradition the invasion, with the murder of Khosrov II by the Parthian prince Anak, took away the Arsacid family's land, and the Persians ruled Armenia until Tiridates's restoration.
nodes.src: Shapur I, ŠKZ (Naqsh-e Rostam, c. 260); Agathangelos; Moses Khorenatsi 2.70–74; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Artagers
nodes.full: In 367–368 Shapur II took Arshak II prisoner, devastated Armenian cities and laid siege to the fortress of Artagers (Artogerassa), which fell after a long siege, when the queen Pharandzem was taken (Faustus says she was put to death); the general Mushegh Mamikonian and the Roman army of Arintheus then recovered Armenia. Faustus gives colourful but unreliable detail.
nodes.src: Ammianus 27.12, 30.1–2; Faustus 4.20–55.

nodes.label: Alans and Huns
nodes.full: Nomads from north of the Caucasus broke through the Darial and Derbent passes into the southern lands several times: the Alans in 72 and 135, when Arrian's army was drawn up against them, and the Huns in 395, who raided Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria as far as Antioch. The Iberian kings kept the Caucasian Gates as a Roman and then Persian charge.
nodes.src: Josephus, Jewish War 7.244–251; Arrian, Order of Battle against the Alans; Jerome, Letter 60.16; Claudian, Against Rufinus 2.

nodes.label: Rhandeia and Nero
nodes.full: The settlement of 63 accepted a Parthian prince on the Armenian throne, but made his rule depend on his receiving the crown from the Roman emperor; Tiridates travelled to Rome, and in 66 was crowned by Nero in a spectacle with a procession through the Forum. The arrangement of a Parthian king under Roman investiture was the model for later treaties.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 15.24–31; Cassius Dio 63.1–7; Suetonius, Nero 13.

nodes.label: Nisibis
nodes.full: After Galerius's victory over Narseh in 298 the peace of Nisibis made the Tigris the border, gave Rome five districts beyond it, confirmed Tiridates in Armenia and set the boundary of Iberia, where the Roman emperor was to appoint the king. It fixed the Caucasian settlement for sixty-five years.
nodes.src: Peter the Patrician, fragment 14 (FHG 4); Ammianus 25.7.9; R. Blockley, East Roman Foreign Policy (1992).

nodes.label: Jovian and partition
nodes.full: After Julian's death in 363 his successor Jovian conceded to Persia the five Tigris districts and Rome's influence over Armenia and Iberia; Shapur then took Armenia in his hand, but Valens's backing of Pap restored a divided protectorate, and in 387 Rome and Persia agreed to partition the kingdom, with one fifth for the Romans and four fifths for the Persians.
nodes.src: Ammianus 25.7, 27.12; Faustus 6.1; Blockley 1992; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Nakharar houses
nodes.full: Armenian society was ordered under the king by great hereditary houses, the nakharars (Mamikonians, Bagratunis, Arzrunis, Kamsarakans, Syunis and others), each with lands, retainers and a hereditary office such as commander (sparapet) or coronant (aspet). Their power over the throne, often supported by Rome or Persia, was the central fact of the kingdom.
nodes.src: Faustus, Epic Histories; Nina Garsoïan, 'The Aristocratic Houses' in Garsoïan 1997; Cyril Toumanoff 1963.

nodes.label: Roman coast forts
nodes.full: Arrian, legate of Cappadocia, in his survey of the Black Sea coast made to Hadrian about 131, lists the Roman garrisons at Apsarus (Gonio), Phasis and Sebastopolis (Dioscurias), and the tribal kings beyond them who held their lands from Rome. The coast was held as the north-eastern limit of the empire.
nodes.src: Arrian, Periplus of the Black Sea 6–18.

nodes.label: Conversion of Armenia
nodes.full: According to Agathangelos, Gregory, a son of the Parthian Anak, who had been imprisoned thirteen years in the pit of Artashat, cured and baptised Tiridates III, who then made Christianity the religion of the kingdom, making Armenia the first state to adopt it. The traditional date is 301; many modern scholars put the king's conversion a decade or so later. Gregory became the first Catholicos.
nodes.src: Agathangelos, History 1–3; Garsoïan, 'The Independent Kingdoms of Medieval Armenia'; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Conversion of Iberia
nodes.full: Rufinus, writing about 400 on the report of an Iberian prince, tells of a captive Christian woman, Nino in Georgian tradition, whose prayers cured a sick child and then the king, who then asked for missionaries from the emperor Constantine. The Georgian chronicles place the event under Mirian III, with a date of c. 326 or c. 337. The first church was the cathedral at Mtskheta.
nodes.src: Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 1.10; Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003; Toumanoff 1963.

nodes.label: Temples of Ashtishat
nodes.full: Agathangelos reports that on conversion the king and Gregory went through the land overthrowing the shrines of the old gods, and at Ashtishat in Taron razed the temples of Vahagn, Anahit and Astghik; the plundered wealth was assigned to the new Church. Archaeology cannot confirm the destruction in detail, and the story reflects the later church's view.
nodes.src: Agathangelos, History (the temples of Ashtishat); Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Nerses and Ashtishat
nodes.full: The Catholicos Nerses I, a descendant of Gregory educated at Caesarea, called about 365 a council at Ashtishat which issued canons, banned consanguineous marriage and traditional mourning, and founded hospitals, hostels and schools. He was killed in 373, according to Faustus, by poison at the king Pap's order.
nodes.src: Faustus, Epic Histories 4.3–5, 5.24; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Albanian church
nodes.full: The Armenian historian Movses Kaghankatvatsi relates that the Albanian king Urnayr was baptised by Gregory the Illuminator and Gregory's grandson Grigoris became the first bishop of Albania, and was martyred among the Caspian tribes in the fourth century. The Albanian church was long under the Armenian Catholicos. These accounts were written centuries later.
nodes.src: Movses Kaghankatvatsi, History of the Albanians 1.12–13; Robert Hewsen, 'The Albanians', Armenian Review.

nodes.label: Garni temple
nodes.full: On a triangular spur above the Azat gorge stands an Ionic peripteral temple of basalt, the only standing Greco-Roman temple in the Caucasus. A Greek inscription of the eleventh year of King Tiridates names him as its builder; the temple, a sun or Mithra temple according to some, was ruined in an earthquake in 1679 and rebuilt in the 1970s.
nodes.src: Garni Greek inscription (Tiridates, 11th year, c. AD 77); Garni excavations (Arakelyan, Trever); Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: First Etchmiadzin
nodes.full: The cathedral of Etchmiadzin, 'where the Only-Begotten descended', is said to have been built by Tiridates and Gregory on the place of a vision, in 303; excavations in 1955–56 found remains of earlier structures below the present building, which has been much rebuilt. It is the mother church of the Armenian Church.
nodes.src: Agathangelos; Etchmiadzin excavations (A. Sahinian, 1955–56); Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Graves of Mtskheta
nodes.full: Cemeteries at Mtskheta, Armaziskhevi, Samtavro and Bagineti contain tombs of rich Iberians with Roman and Parthian gold, silver, glass and gems, such as the silver cup of Pitiaxes Bersuma, as well as bronze and imported pottery. They show Iberia as a prosperous, outward-facing kingdom in the Roman period.
nodes.src: Archaeological excavations at Mtskheta (Apakidze, Lordkipanidze); Georgian National Museum.

nodes.label: Mingachevir
nodes.full: At Mingachevir on the middle Kura, a settlement and burial ground with pottery kilns, glass, ornaments and large jars made in the first centuries AD give the best archaeological picture of Albanian craft and trade, with imported glass and coins from Rome and Parthia and Sasanian Persia.
nodes.src: Mingachevir Archaeological Expedition reports (1946–); Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Armenian alphabet
nodes.full: The cleric Mesrop Mashtots, with the Catholicos Sahak and King Vramshapuh, created in about 405 an alphabet of thirty-six letters for Armenian, after journeys to Syrian and Greek lands to find a script that could render its sounds. The first text translated was a verse of Proverbs, and the Bible followed within a generation. It became the instrument of Armenian literature and national identity.
nodes.src: Koriun, Life of Mashtots; Moses Khorenatsi 3.47–54; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Agathangelos
nodes.full: The History attributed to Agathangelos, written in Armenian in the later fifth century with Greek and Syriac versions, tells the story of Tiridates, Gregory's imprisonment, the martyrdom of the virgins Hripsime and Gayane, and the conversion; it became the founding narrative of the Armenian Church and the principal source for the event.
nodes.src: Agathangelos, History of the Armenians (trans. R. Thomson, 1976).

nodes.label: Tacitus and Dio
nodes.full: The Roman accounts of the wars for Armenia, Tacitus in the Annals (books 11–15) and Cassius Dio, give the fullest narrative of the first century and Verus's war, based on official dispatches and Corbulo's own memoirs. They see Armenia as an object of Roman policy and know its people only vaguely.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 11–15; Cassius Dio 62–63, 68, 71.

nodes.label: Albanian script
nodes.full: Koriun and Movses Kaghankatvatsi credit Mesrop Mashtots with devising an alphabet for the Albanians as well as the Armenians and Georgians, about 410; a script of fifty-two letters has been identified in a palimpsest discovered at St Catherine's monastery on Sinai in 1975 and deciphered in the 2000s. It is the only substantial record of the Albanian language, of which Udi is the closest living relative.
nodes.src: Koriun, Life of Mashtots 16; Movses Kaghankatvatsi 1.27; Zaza Aleksidze et al., Catalogue of the Albanian Palimpsests, Sinai (2009).

nodes.label: Armazi inscription
nodes.full: A bilingual stele of the second century in Greek and Aramaic, found at Armaziskhevi in 1940, commemorates Serapita, pitiaxes (viceroy) of Iberia, and her father Zevakh; it uses the Aramaic-derived script called Armazic, whose relation to the later Georgian alphabet is debated. It is the main inscription of royal Iberia.
nodes.src: Armazi bilingual inscription (Georgian National Museum); Toumanoff 1963.

nodes.label: Caspian–Phasis road
nodes.full: Pliny says that Indian goods were carried to the Caspian by way of the Oxus, then taken up the Kura and a five-day overland road to the Phasis in Colchis, and to the Black Sea. The route lay through Iberia and was a source of its wealth, as were the Roman and Parthian coins found in its graves and hoards.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 6.52; Strabo 11.7.3; Toumanoff 1963.

nodes.label: Roman coin
nodes.full: Hoards of Roman denarii and Parthian drachms found in Armenia and Georgia show the use of Roman silver, possibly as subsidy payments to the client kings and, by trade, to the highland markets. Iberia has some of the largest hoards.
nodes.src: Numismatic hoard publications (Georgian National Museum); Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Nakharar estates
nodes.full: The great noble houses held extensive lands, villages and their dependent peasantry, as indicated by Faustus and the Armenian chronicles, with royal domains and temple lands taken by the church; peasants (shinakan) worked on them and owed service to the lords. The nobility's wealth was agricultural and based on vineyards, grain and herds.
nodes.src: Faustus, Epic Histories; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Bath of Garni
nodes.full: Beside the temple the Roman-style bath of Garni has a heated floor on hypocausts, a stone-lined pool and a mosaic floor of marine figures, Oceanus and Thalassa, with fish and sea-creatures, made of local pebbles, stones and glass. It is one of the few Roman bathing buildings of the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Garni excavations (B. Arakelyan, 1949–1950s).

nodes.label: Vagharshapat and Dvin
nodes.full: After Artaxata was razed in 163, the kings used Vagharshapat (Kainepolis), where Etchmiadzin lies, and Khosrov III Kotak moved the court in about 335 to Dvin on the Araxes plain, a fortified town with a palace and a citadel, which became the Armenian capital for centuries. The kings founded the new cities as centres of royal administration.
nodes.src: Moses Khorenatsi 3.8; Dvin excavations (K. Ghafadaryan, 1937–).

nodes.label: Syriac and Greek missions
nodes.full: Armenian Christianity drew on Syriac missionaries from Edessa and Nisibis and on Greek Cappadocia, where Gregory was said to have been raised, and later on the church of Caesarea; Iberia's first priests came from Antioch or Constantinople. The two churches adopted a different liturgical language from their neighbours.
nodes.src: Garsoïan 1997; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Sasanian suzerainty
nodes.full: Shapur I's inscription of c. 260 lists the kings of Armenia, Iberia and Albania as his vassals, up to the Caucasus gates, and later Sasanian kings set marzbans over Armenia and governors over Albania, with Zoroastrian priests and fire temples as instruments. The Persian presence set the model for later rule.
nodes.src: Shapur I, ŠKZ; Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996).

nodes.label: Three-way struggle
nodes.full: For four centuries the highlands were the principal object of the conflict of Rome and, after 224, of the Sasanian empire, with Armenia, Iberia and Albania as the buffer states between them. The overthrow of the Parthians by the Sasanians in 224 converted a rivalry of related dynasties into one of rival empires and faiths.
nodes.src: Garsoïan 1997; Blockley 1992; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Mosaic signed by labourers
nodes.full: In the bath of Garni a Greek line set in the mosaic reads 'We worked and found no reward', either a rueful statement by the workers or the words of one of them. It is a rare statement by labourers of the Caucasus, set in the floor of a bath for the court.
nodes.src: Garni bath mosaic inscription (Greek); Garni excavations.

nodes.label: Nino
nodes.full: Rufinus describes the Christian apostle of Iberia as a woman taken captive among the Iberians, who lived there with a strict regimen of prayer and fasting; the Georgian sources make her a Cappadocian relative of Saint George. The central part played by a captive woman in the conversion of a kingdom has been much discussed.
nodes.src: Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 1.10; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Pharandzem
nodes.full: Pharandzem, wife of Gnel and then of the king Arshak II, was held with the royal treasure in Artagers while her husband was a prisoner; Faustus tells of her command of the garrison and of her death after its fall, taken by the Persians. She is the best known woman of the Arsacid court.
nodes.src: Faustus, Epic Histories 4.44, 4.55.

nodes.label: The Roman arrival and the last Artaxiads
nodes.full: By 1 BC Armenia, Iberia and Albania were client or neighbouring kingdoms of the Roman frontier and Armenia was a field between Rome and Parthia.
nodes.src: background — see the Hellenistic Caucasus folio (hellenistic-caucasus-330bc-1bc)
